warmup.q: A shop's website runs on a server with 16 cores. Every checkout gets its own thread from a pool of 200, and each checkout takes 200 ms, almost all of it waiting for the bank to answer. Traffic rises from 800 to 1,500 checkouts a second. What happens?
options: Every core gets busy, and each checkout gets a little slower
The shop finishes about 1,000 checkouts a second and no more, the line of waiting checkouts keeps growing, and most cores sit idle
The pool starts more threads to keep up
Nothing much: 200 threads can handle any rate, as long as each checkout is short
warmup.why: Each checkout holds a thread for 200 ms, so one thread finishes 5 checkouts a second and 200 threads finish 1,000. The other 500 a second wait in the pool's queue, and that line grows every second. Most cores have nothing to do, because the threads are waiting, not computing. A fixed pool never adds threads on its own. The first two sections work through it.

opening:
Picture a restaurant with an odd rule. Every table gets its own waiter, from the first menu to the bill. The waiter takes the order, then stands at the kitchen door until the food is ready. Most of a waiter's evening is spent admiring that door.

The restaurant has 200 waiters. On a busy night, the 201st party waits outside, while nearly every waiter stands idle by the kitchen. Hiring is slow, because each new waiter needs a contract, a uniform and a locker.

Many Java servers run like that restaurant. Each request gets one thread, one path of work through the program, for its whole life, and mostly the thread waits for other programs to answer. The trap is easy to fall into, because the code is the plainest kind there is. It passes every test and fails only at the busiest hour.

Pools in production tuned our thread pools with care, and still a pool of waiting threads hits a wall. In this lesson, we'll find that wall with arithmetic, see why more threads can't fix it, weigh the old way around it and meet virtual threads. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with waiters who mostly stood at the kitchen door. The shop's checkout did the same: 195 of its 200 ms were waiting, so 200 threads stopped at 1,000 a second while most cores sat idle. More platform threads cost too much, and async code costs the plain style. Virtual threads keep the code and make the waiting cheap.

Now pick a pool in your own code and write down its thread count and how long a request holds one of its threads. Divide the first by the second. That's your wall, in requests per second.

Next, we'll open a virtual thread. How do 2,000 sleeping threads share four cores, and where does a waiting thread's stack go?

sections.h: One checkout, one thread: why 200 threads stop at 1,000 a second
sections.html:
Let's give the restaurant a program. A small shop sells online, and its website handles checkouts. To check out one basket, the program reads the request and asks the stock service whether the items are in the warehouse. Then it asks the bank to take the payment, saves the order in the shop's database and writes the reply.

A service here is a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. The bank's service is our old friend, the slow web service from Threads from zero, still taking 120 ms. A database is the program that stores the shop's data, such as its orders.

Now add up one checkout. Reading the request takes 2 ms, the stock service 40 ms, the bank 120 ms, the database 35 ms and the reply 3 ms. That's 200 ms, and only 5 ms of it runs on the CPU, the processor. The other 195 ms is waiting. The figure below shows the shape.

The program gives each checkout one thread from a pool of 200. A pool is a fixed team of threads that take tasks from a queue, a line of waiting tasks, like the kitchen in the executors track. The thread stays with its checkout from the first line to the reply. That style is called thread-per-request, and it's the restaurant's personal waiter.

Each of those threads is a platform thread, the kind Java has always had. A platform thread is a Java thread backed by one thread of the operating system, the program that runs every other program and shares out the processor. We'll see what that costs in a moment.

While the thread waits for the bank, it is blocked: it can't go on until the answer arrives. A blocked thread does no work, but no other checkout can use it.

That one fact sets the wall. One thread finishes a checkout every 0.2 s, so 5 a second. 200 threads finish 1,000 a second, and not one more.

At 800 checkouts a second, 160 threads are busy and 40 sit idle. Then traffic rises to 1,500 a second. The idle threads fill at once, and the other 500 checkouts each second wait in the pool's queue. After 10 seconds, 5,000 are waiting, and a new checkout waits 5 seconds before a thread even picks it up.

And the processor? Each thread spends one fortieth of its time on the CPU, so at any moment only about 5 of the 200 threads are running code. A server with 16 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, has 11 cores with nothing to do. Anyone watching the server sees a slow shop on a bored machine.

Let's watch the wall in a smaller model. WallDemo, in the Try it below, runs 2,000 fake checkouts that each just call Thread.sleep for 100 ms, standing in for the waits. First it runs them on a pool of 100 threads. Predict before you read on: 100 threads at 0.1 s each finish 1,000 a second, so 2,000 checkouts should take about 2 seconds. On this 4-core machine, while other heavy programs were running, the first line said:

fixed pool of 100           2,000 requests in  2,229 ms  =      897 requests/s

That's the prediction, plus a little start-up time. The demo prints a second line too, and we'll come back to it in the last section.

The wall comes from two numbers: how many threads there are, and how long each request holds one. That arithmetic has a name, and it works for much more than threads.

code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** * Runs N fake checkout requests that each block for a while, * first on a fixed pool, then with one virtual thread per request. * * <p>Args: pool size, number of requests, latency in ms. Default: 100 2000 100. */ public class WallDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int poolSize = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 100; int requests = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 2_000; Duration latency = Duration.ofMillis(args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 100); Runnable checkout = () -> { try { Thread.sleep(latency); // stands in for the waits on the bank and the database } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize)) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) pool.execute(checkout); } report("fixed pool of " + poolSize, requests, t0); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) perTask.execute(checkout); } report("virtual thread per task", requests, t1); } static void report(String label, int requests, long startNanos) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - startNanos) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-26s %,6d requests in %,6d ms = %,8.0f requests/s%n", label, requests, ms, requests * 1000.0 / Math.max(ms, 1)); } }

try.expect: 100 threads at 100 ms finish at most 1,000 checkouts a second, so 2,000 take about 2 s (busy runs here: 2,094 to 2,229 ms). 200 threads halve that to about 1 s (1,126 ms here). The pool's speed is its thread count divided by the time each checkout holds a thread.

aside.title: Is 200 threads a number anyone really uses?
aside.html: Yes, it's a common default. If you write web services in Java, a web server such as Tomcat, the program that receives each request and hands it to your code, runs it on a thread from a pool. Tomcat's pool stops at 200 threads unless you change it, and Spring Boot, a popular framework that runs on Tomcat, keeps the same default. So a plain Java web service often meets this wall at this very number. Since Spring Boot 3.2, the setting spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs requests on virtual threads instead. Lesson 6 of this track covers moving a service over.

sections.h: Little's law: how many checkouts are inside at once
sections.html:
Sizing a pool met a law from ticket windows. It's worth meeting again, because this whole track leans on it. Little's law says that in any stable system, one where on average as many leave as arrive:

L = λ × W
inside at once = arrival rate × time each one spends inside

L is how many are inside at once. λ (the Greek letter lambda) is the arrival rate, how many arrive each second. W is how long each one stays, from arriving to leaving. For a request, that time is its latency.

With thread-per-request, every checkout inside holds one thread, so L is also the number of threads we need. At 1,500 checkouts a second and 0.2 s each:

L = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300 checkouts inside = 300 threads

We have 200. Turn the law around, and it gives the most a pool can finish each second, its throughput:

λ max = L / W = 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 checkouts per second

The formula gives the same wall as the last section, and now we can change the numbers in it.

Say the bank has a slow afternoon. Its answers take 1.2 seconds instead of 120 ms, so W grows from 0.2 s to 1.28 s. The same 200 threads now finish at most 200 / 1.28 = 156 checkouts a second. Nobody changed a line of our code, and the shop just lost five sixths of its capacity.

A slow service elsewhere brings down a thread-per-request program this way. Each waiting checkout holds its thread for longer, so the threads run out sooner, and the CPU has even less to do.

WallDemo agrees. With a 300 ms sleep instead of 100 ms (-Pargs='100 2000 300'), the pool's time should triple, to about 6 seconds:

fixed pool of 100           2,000 requests in  6,198 ms  =      323 requests/s

It did. When the work is mostly waiting, a pool's throughput is its threads divided by the latency, and faster cores wouldn't move it at all.

A slow service you call makes your own capacity smaller. Measure W on a bad day, not a good one.

That leaves two ways out. We can make W smaller, which we often can't, because the bank isn't ours. Or we can make each checkout cheaper to hold while it waits.

The quickest-sounding way to do that is to hire more waiters. So why not run 2,000 threads?

try.title: Size a service by hand, then check the demo
steps: A shop's search page gets 600 requests a second, and each one waits 250 ms for a slow service. How many requests are inside at once?
The page runs on a pool of 64 threads. What's the most it can finish per second, and how fast does the queue grow?
Predict the pool's time in WallDemo with a 300 ms sleep, then run ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l01.WallDemo -Pargs='100 2000 300'.

sections.h: Why not more threads: what a platform thread costs
sections.html:
If waiting threads are the problem, the obvious fix is more of them. Make the pool 2,000 threads, and even the bank's slow afternoon is covered. The trouble is the kind of thread.

Every thread in our pool is a platform thread, and the operating system does real work for each one. When you call start(), Java asks the operating system for a new thread. That's a system call, a request from a program to the operating system, and it isn't cheap.

The operating system also reserves the thread's stack, the memory where a thread keeps the method calls it's in the middle of and their local variables. On 64-bit Linux, Java reserves 1 MB for each stack by default (the -Xss setting). The operating system hands out the memory only as the stack really grows, but the reservation and its bookkeeping stay for the thread's whole life.

Then the operating system has to share out the cores. With thousands of threads, it spends more and more time switching between them. Each switch also throws away part of the CPU's cache, its small fast copy of recently used memory.

The contract, the uniform and the locker from the opening are these costs, and every waiter pays them, even one who only stands at the kitchen door.

ThreadCostDemo, in the Try it below, measures them. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it lets them go. Then it does the same with 100,000 virtual threads, the new kind this lesson ends with. Which do you expect to finish first? On this busy machine, one run printed:

platform   4,000 threads alive at once: started in 6,644 ms, all finished after 7,454 ms (1863.5 us per thread)
virtual  100,000 threads alive at once: started in   585 ms, all finished after 2,571 ms (25.7 us per thread)

Twenty-five times as many virtual threads finished in a third of the time. The cost per platform thread swings with how busy the machine is: another run here gave 268 microseconds, not 1,864. It still stayed many times above the virtual threads' 19 to 26 microseconds.

So a JVM is comfortable with hundreds of platform threads and survives a few thousand. At tens of thousands, it starts fighting the operating system's limits on threads and memory. A million is out of reach.

A platform thread is an operating system thread. You can have thousands, not millions.

Here the restaurant picture breaks, and not in our favor. A real waiter at the kitchen door might refill a glass on the way. A blocked platform thread can do nothing else at all until its answer arrives.

So more threads can't carry us far. The next idea is older than virtual threads: stop holding a thread while we wait.

try.title: Count what a thread costs
steps: Run ThreadCostDemo with the command below. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it releases them, then 100,000 virtual threads.
Before you look at the output, guess which run finishes first: 4,000 platform threads, or 25 times as many virtual threads?
Try -Pargs='5000 1000000' for a million virtual threads. Keep the platform count at 5,000 or less on a laptop.

code.title: ThreadCostDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * * <p>Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ public class ThreadCostDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int platform = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4_000; int virtual = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 100_000; time("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()); time("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()); } static void time(String kind, int n, Thread.Builder builder) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(n); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { threads.add(builder.start(() -> { try { release.await(); // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } })); } long startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; release.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); long totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)%n", kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n); } }

alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * * Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val platform = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 4_000 val virtual = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 100_000 startAndRelease("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()) startAndRelease("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()) } private fun startAndRelease(kind: String, n: Int, builder: Thread.Builder) { val release = CountDownLatch(1) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(n) { builder.start { try { release.await() // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } val startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 release.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } val totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)" .format(kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n)) }

try.expect: Each platform thread costs tens to hundreds of microseconds to start, and more on a busy machine (268 and 1,864 microseconds in two runs here). Each virtual thread costs a few tens of microseconds or less, so 100,000 of them finish sooner than 4,000 platform threads. A million virtual threads take longer and use some heap, but nothing crashes.

sections.h: Giving the thread back while it waits: async code, and what it costs
sections.html:
The first way around the wall was to stop holding a thread during a wait. In the restaurant, that's one waiter running between many tables with a notepad. Table 4's soup is ready, so bring the bread. The bank said yes for table 9, so print the bill. Nobody stands at the door, and a few waiters serve every table.

In code, the notepad is a chain of steps to run later. Here's the checkout both ways. Both versions make the same three calls in the same order:

Java
// blocking: one thread per checkout, held for all 200 ms
Receipt checkout(Basket basket) {
    Stock stock = warehouse.reserve(basket);         // 40 ms
    Payment paid = bank.charge(basket, stock);       // 120 ms
    return orders.save(basket, paid);                // 35 ms
}

// async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait
CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkoutAsync(Basket basket) {
    return warehouse.reserveAsync(basket)
        .thenCompose(stock -> bank.chargeAsync(basket, stock))
        .thenCompose(paid -> orders.saveAsync(basket, paid));
}
Kotlin
// blocking: one thread per checkout, held for all 200 ms
fun checkout(basket: Basket): Receipt {
    val stock = warehouse.reserve(basket)            // 40 ms
    val paid = bank.charge(basket, stock)            // 120 ms
    return orders.save(basket, paid)                 // 35 ms
}

// async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait
fun checkoutAsync(basket: Basket): CompletableFuture<Receipt> =
    warehouse.reserveAsync(basket)
        .thenCompose { stock -> bank.chargeAsync(basket, stock) }
        .thenCompose { paid -> orders.saveAsync(basket, paid) }

A CompletableFuture, from the executors track, is a box for a result that arrives later. Read thenCompose as "when this box is filled, start the next step and hand me its box". No thread waits for the bank. When its answer comes, it starts the next step on whatever thread is free.

A program built this way can keep thousands of checkouts going at once on a few threads. Often it has one event loop per core: a thread that runs many requests' small steps in turn and must never block. It works, and it's why async libraries, and the reactive ones built on the same idea (a later track covers them), became popular. The price is paid in the code.

Every library on the checkout's path must be async too, including the one that talks to the database. One ordinary blocking call on an event loop stalls every request that shares that loop, and nothing warns you.

The call stack stops telling the story. When the bank's step fails, the stack trace lists pool threads and lambdas, which is everything except what happened. A debugger can't step from one stage to the next.

Control flow turns into method calls. A try/catch becomes exceptionally, and a loop with an early exit becomes a chain that calls itself. A ThreadLocal is a variable with a separate value for each thread. It doesn't follow the checkout from thread to thread, so anything kept in one, such as the current customer, gets lost on the way.

Kotlin coroutines get closest to the blocking style. A suspend function, which the compiler can pause at a wait and resume later on any thread, reads top to bottom like checkout. But coroutines need libraries that suspend instead of block. A blocking database call inside a coroutine blocks a real thread, and we're back to sizing a pool: Dispatchers.IO, the coroutine library's shared pool for blocking calls.

If your code is already async and works, keep it. Rewriting plain blocking code as chains just to save threads is a poor trade.

Check yourself: an async service runs on 8 event loops, and someone adds a blocking 50 ms database call to one handler. How many of those requests can the service serve per second? At most 160. Each loop is stuck for the whole 50 ms of every call, so Little's law with L = 8 and W = 0.05 s gives 8 / 0.05 = 160, however fast the CPU is.

Async code frees the thread by changing the code. What if, instead, threads were so cheap that a waiting one didn't matter?

sections.h: Virtual threads: cheap threads for the same blocking code
sections.html:
JDK 21 took the other way out: it made threads cheap. Virtual threads became a final feature in JDK 21, no longer an experiment you had to switch on. They came through JEP 444, a JDK Enhancement Proposal: the design document for a change to Java.

A virtual thread is a normal java.lang.Thread that the JDK schedules instead of the operating system. It runs on a small pool of platform threads, about one per core. When it blocks, for example on a network read or a sleep, the JDK sets it aside. It keeps the thread's stack on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, and lends the platform thread to another virtual thread. The next lesson, How virtual threads work, opens that up.

In the restaurant, that's a waiter who costs next to nothing to hire. Every table can keep its personal waiter again, and a waiter standing at the kitchen door is no longer a waste.

So we keep the blocking checkout method, and give every checkout its own virtual thread. Both versions start one new virtual thread per basket:

Java
try (ExecutorService perCheckout = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (Basket basket : incoming) {
        perCheckout.submit(() -> checkout(basket));   // blocking code, cheap thread
    }
}   // close() waits for every task
Kotlin
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perCheckout ->
    for (basket in incoming) {
        perCheckout.submit(Callable { checkout(basket) })   // blocking code, cheap thread
    }
}   // use {} closes the executor, and close() waits for every task

The executor starts a brand-new virtual thread for every task and keeps none around. Remember the second line of WallDemo? Here it is, from the same run as the first:

fixed pool of 100           2,000 requests in  2,229 ms  =      897 requests/s
virtual thread per task     2,000 requests in    268 ms  =    7,463 requests/s

All 2,000 checkouts slept at the same time, so the run took a little over one sleep. With the 300 ms sleep, it took 391 ms. The time follows the latency of one checkout, not the number of checkouts.

Little's law still holds. At 1,500 checkouts a second and 0.2 s each, 300 are still inside at once. They just don't cost 300 operating system threads. When the bank slows to 1.2 s, 1,920 are inside, and that's fine too.

Be clear about what virtual threads don't change:

  • One checkout is not faster. It still waits 200 ms. Virtual threads give scale (more checkouts waiting at once), not speed.
  • Work that computes gains nothing. With 16 cores, at most 16 threads compute at once, virtual or not.
  • Limits elsewhere stay. The shop's database still accepts 20 connections, open lines to it, at once. With the thread cap gone, 300 checkouts reach it together, and the queue moves there. Lesson 3 of this track puts a limit in front of it.

A few kinds of code can also keep a virtual thread from letting go of its platform thread. Lesson 4 of this track covers them.

Virtual threads give scale, not speed. Each checkout waits as long as before, but many more can wait at once.

The restaurant picture breaks here too: the kitchen is still the kitchen. If the slow part is the cooking itself, or a grill with room for only 20 pans, cheaper waiters don't help.

The lab turns the wall into something you can measure: the same blocking handler on a fixed pool, and on one virtual thread per task.

compare.title: Blocking code that scales: virtual threads and coroutines

java.title: Java 21+: virtual threads
java.html: // plain blocking code, one cheap virtual thread per checkout List<Receipt> checkoutAll(List<Basket> baskets) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Basket b : baskets) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> checkout(b))); List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } } Receipt checkout(Basket b) { Stock stock = warehouse.reserve(b); // an ordinary blocking call over the network Payment paid = bank.charge(b, stock); return orders.save(b, paid); // an ordinary database call }

kotlin.title: Kotlin: kotlinx.coroutines
kotlin.html: // suspend functions: the compiler turns them into steps it can pause between suspend fun checkoutAll(baskets: List<Basket>): List<Receipt> = coroutineScope { baskets.map { b -> async { checkout(b) } }.awaitAll() } suspend fun checkout(b: Basket): Receipt { val stock = warehouse.reserve(b) // must itself suspend to free the thread val paid = bank.charge(b, stock) return orders.save(b, paid) // a blocking database call here would block a real thread }

compare.note: Both read top to bottom, and both keep thousands of checkouts going at once on a few operating system threads. The difference is where the pausing happens. Kotlin does it in the compiler: only suspend functions can give the thread back, so every waiting call on the path has to be suspend-aware, and a blocking database call needs withContext(Dispatchers.IO), which is a thread pool again. Virtual threads do it in the JDK while the program runs: most blocking JDK calls (network reads, sleep, locks, a BlockingQueue) set the virtual thread aside, so existing database drivers and HTTP clients (libraries that call web services) work unchanged. The two also mix: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() runs coroutines on virtual threads, which helps when they call blocking libraries.

worked.title: Size the checkout service with Little's law

steps.say: Write down W for one checkout, step by step. Use typical times for a first pass, and redo it later with the times from a bad day.
steps.code:
read request   2 ms  (CPU)
stock         40 ms  (network, waiting)
bank         120 ms  (network, waiting)
database      35 ms  (database, waiting)
reply          3 ms  (CPU)
W            200 ms

steps.say: Work out L at the busiest hour. That's how many checkouts are inside at once, so it's how many threads thread-per-request needs.

Compare with the pool you have. 200 threads cap the shop at 1,000 checkouts a second. With 1,500 arriving, the queue grows by 500 every second. After 10 s, 5,000 are queued, and a new checkout waits about 5 s before a thread even picks it up.
steps.code:
λ max = 200 / 0.200 s = 1,000/s
queue growth = 1,500 - 1,000 = 500 per second
wait after 10 s = 5,000 / 1,000/s = 5 s

steps.say: Apply the same law to everything a checkout holds, not just threads. The database step holds a connection, an open line to the database, for 35 ms. With 20 connections, that step alone caps the shop at 571 checkouts a second. More platform threads, or virtual threads, would only move the queue to the connections.
steps.code:
connections needed = 1,500/s × 0.035 s = 53
λ max (database)   = 20 / 0.035 s = 571/s   <- the real bottleneck

steps.say: Decide. Raise the connection count only if the database can take 53 at once. Then make threads cheap with virtual threads, and keep an explicit limit in front of the database. Lesson 3 of this track shows that limit.

lab.title: Measure the wall: fixed pool vs a virtual thread per task
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Write LittlesLaw.inFlight (L = λ × W) and LittlesLaw.maxThroughput (λ = L / W). Turn the Duration into seconds as a double first.

Write BlockingRunner.runOnFixedPool: open Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize) in a try-with-resources block, execute the handler tasks times, and count each finished task in an AtomicInteger. Return the count after the try block.

Run the tests again. The test's FakeSlowCall is the handler: it sleeps like a call to a slow service and counts how many calls run at once. The last test takes about 2.5 s: 2,000 calls of 100 ms on a 100-thread pool, then on virtual threads. Read its assertions to see why the pool can never beat 2 s.
hints: close() on an ExecutorService (JDK 19 and later) calls shutdown() and then waits for every task. That's why the try-with-resources block makes your method wait.
Count with an AtomicInteger, not an int: the tasks finish on many threads at once. The lesson "Race conditions: why count++ lies" shows what count++ does there.
Duration.toNanos() / 1_000_000_000.0 gives seconds as a double without losing the milliseconds.
lab.done: All five tests in ThreadPerRequestTest pass, two runs in a row.

drill.title: Little's law and the per-task executor, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A shop's order-tracking page gets 400 requests a second, and each request waits 300 ms for the delivery company's web service. (1) How many requests are inside at once? (2) A pool of 50 threads serves them: what's the most it can finish per second? (3) Write a method that runs each Runnable in a list on its own virtual thread, and returns when all of them are done.

answer.html: // (1) L = 400/s × 0.3 s = 120 inside at once // (2) λ max = 50 / 0.3 s = about 167 requests per second, far below 400 // (3) static void runAll(List<Runnable> tasks) { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (Runnable r : tasks) perTask.execute(r); } // close() waits for all of them }

alt.html: // (1) L = 400/s × 0.3 s = 120 inside at once // (2) λ max = 50 / 0.3 s = about 167 requests per second, far below 400 // (3) fun runAll(tasks: List<Runnable>) { Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> tasks.forEach { perTask.execute(it) } } // close() waits for all of them }

recap: A platform thread is one operating system thread, with a 1 MB stack reserved by default on 64-bit Linux. A JVM handles thousands of them, not millions.
Thread-per-request gives each request one thread for its whole life, waits included. A blocked thread does no work, but nobody else can use it.
Little's law: requests inside = arrival rate × latency. Turned around, threads divided by latency is the most a blocking service can finish per second, and a slow service you call lowers it.
Async code gives the thread back at every wait, at the price of async-only libraries, stack traces without the story and lost ThreadLocal values.
Virtual threads (final in JDK 21, JEP 444) make threads cheap, so plain blocking code can keep thousands of requests waiting at once.
The limit: they give scale, not speed. One request is no faster, computing gains nothing, and limits elsewhere, such as a database's 20 connections, become the new wall.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why the shop's website tops out at about 1,000 checkouts a second while most of its cores sit idle. Explain it with Little's law, and say what virtual threads would change and what they wouldn't.
explain.answer: Each checkout takes about 200 ms, and almost all of that is waiting for the stock service, the bank and the database. With thread-per-request, a checkout holds its thread the whole time, so 200 threads can finish at most 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 checkouts a second. Above that, checkouts queue for a thread and latency climbs, while the cores have almost nothing to do, because the threads are waiting, not computing. Virtual threads make threads cheap, so we could keep 300 or 3,000 checkouts waiting at once without 3,000 operating system threads, and the thread cap goes away. They wouldn't make any single checkout faster, and the next limit would be the database's connections and the bank's own capacity, so we'd need explicit limits there.

deeper.html:
Little's law needs only one assumption: the system is stable, meaning that over the long run requests leave as fast as they arrive. It says nothing about the shape of the traffic or the order of service, which is why it works for a shop's checkout as well as for a supermarket.

It doesn't tell you what happens near the limit. As a pool gets close to 100% busy, the queue doesn't grow smoothly. Short bursts above the average rate make requests wait, and the waits add up faster than the load. A pool that is busy 95% of the time has much longer queues than one at 80%, even though it is only a little busier. That's why people who plan capacity leave room to spare.

It also explains why thread-per-request lasted so long. If W is 5 ms (a lookup in memory), 200 threads give you 40,000 requests a second, and nobody needs async code. The wall only appears when W is mostly waiting for other programs, which describes most services that call other services. The motivation section of JEP 444 makes this same argument: the number of threads limits throughput long before the CPU or the network do.

One honest question remains: why not shrink the stack with -Xss and run 20,000 platform threads? Some teams did. You still pay a system call for every thread you start, the operating system still has to schedule 20,000 threads, and a stack that's too small turns a deep chain of calls into a StackOverflowError. A virtual thread's stack lives on the heap and grows only as deep as the code really goes, so you don't have to guess a size.
